content: It is determined by the cardiac output (CO) and systemic vascular resistance (SVR). Maintaining normal BP is essential for proper blood circulation throughout the cardiovascular system. In clinical practice, BP is considered one of the most critical vital signs. However, lower BP thresholds are recommended for certain populations, such as individuals with diabetes or significant kidney disease. In 2004, the Seventh Report of the Joint National Committee (JNC 7) categorized BP into four groups: normal, prehypertension, stage I hypertension, and stage II hypertension. In contrast, the European Society of Hypertension (ESH) and the European Society of Cardiology (ESC) introduced a seven-category classification in 2007, which was reaffirmed in 2013. Unlike JNC 7, the ESH/ESC classification excludes the prehypertension category and instead divides hypertension into three grades. The exact mechanisms underlying primary (essential) hypertension remain unclear, though it is widely accepted that it results from a combination of genetic and environmental factors, with varying contributions among individuals. Secondary hypertension, which accounts for only 5-10% of cases, has identifiable causes such as obstructive sleep apnea, hyperaldosteronism, kidney diseases, excessive catecholamine production, coarctation of the aorta, and Cushing syndrome. When no specific cause is found, the condition is classified as primary hypertension, which is a chronic disease requiring lifelong management. Before diagnosing primary hypertension, secondary causes must be excluded. Other conditions that can elevate BP, such as white coat hypertension, masked hypertension, and pseudohypertension, should also be considered. Hypertension is a global epidemic and one of the most prevalent chronic diseases. Data from the 2011-2012 National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) showed an age-adjusted prevalence of 29.1% among U.S. adults aged 18 and older. In Europe, the prevalence is estimated at 44%. Hypertension is more common in older adults and non-Hispanic Black individuals, but its prevalence is similar between men and women. Risk factors for essential hypertension include advanced age, male sex, African American ethnicity, dyslipidemia, diabetes mellitus, smoking, high dietary salt intake, obesity, and a sedentary lifestyle. Emerging risk factors are also being studied. Screening for hypertension typically begins between the ages of 13 and 20, depending on the guidelines. While hypertension is generally defined as SBP > 140 mmHg and/or DBP > 90 mmHg, lower thresholds may apply to specific populations. Hypertension is a major risk factor for serious conditions, including cardiovascular disease, stroke, kidney disease, and retinal damage. Chronic uncontrolled hypertension can lead to target organ damage, with the heart, brain, kidneys, and eyes being the most commonly affected organs. Even moderate BP elevations can reduce life expectancy and increase the risk of cardiovascular complications. BP should not be viewed as discrete stages but rather as a continuum of risk. Management decisions should consider the overall cardiovascular risk profile, not just BP values in isolation. A detailed medical history is essential for diagnosing and assessing hypertension. History-taking should focus on identifying symptoms of high BP, risk factors, and evidence of target organ damage. In some cases, history alone can reveal secondary causes, such as drug-induced hypertension, guiding further evaluation and management. Physical examination findings in patients with isolated hypertension are often unremarkable, except for elevated BP. However, clinicians should carefully assess for signs of target organ damage or associated conditions. Proper technique, including appropriate cuff size and patient positioning, is essential to avoid errors. Laboratory tests are performed to identify secondary causes of hypertension and assess for end-organ damage. These tests may include evaluations for diabetes, dyslipidemia, and kidney function, as these conditions are both risk factors and potential complications of hypertension. Electrocardiography (ECG) is used to detect left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) or silent myocardial infarction. Echocardiography can provide additional information, such as evidence of LVH or heart failure. A chest X-ray may reveal signs of congestive heart failure, including cardiomegaly, pulmonary edema, or Kerley B lines. Initial treatment for hypertension typically involves lifestyle modifications, which are also crucial for prevention. Recommended changes include reducing dietary salt intake, achieving or maintaining a healthy weight, increasing consumption of fruits, vegetables, and low-fat dairy products, limiting alcohol intake, and engaging in regular aerobic exercise. While lifestyle changes can effectively control BP in many patients, most will require two or more antihypertensive medications. Pharmacologic therapy is the most effective way to lower BP in hypertensive patients. Guidelines from JNC 7 (2004) and ESH/ESC (2013) provide recommendations for medical management. Recent evidence has shifted away from the traditional use of thiazide diuretics as first-line therapy for isolated essential hypertension. Current guidelines support the use of any antihypertensive agent, with specific drug classes recommended for certain conditions or patient populations.
